newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Businesses are fleeing Nigeria, warns industry.
newsitem.headline: Businesses are fleeing Nigeria, warns industry.

text.p: Nigeria's industry chief on Wednesday warned the military rulers that businesses were leaving Africa's most populous country and urged them to act to halt the trend.

"Already, reports reaching us indicate that companies are dismantling their plants and moving to Asia, Latin America and even some African countries where the business environment is more favourable," Rufus Giwa, president of the Manufacturers Association of Nigeria (MAN), said.
"This is a trend that must be checked immediately by reversing the obnoxious policies," Giwa said in an address to an industry function in Lagos read on his behalf by MAN director-general Uzor Okeke.
Among the policies Giwa complained of are arbitrary taxes by various tiers of government and physical closure of companies to make them pay up.
"The stiffling effects of these measures are compounding the harsh industrial operating conditions in the country," he said.
Nigeria has been in crisis since 1993 when the military annulled a presidential election that would have ushered in civil rule democracy.
Businessman Moshood Abiola, who was on course to win the polls has been in detention since June 1994 for declaring himself president in defiance of the military.
The political crisis turned foreign investors away to other destinations such as South Africa, which was just coming out of international isolation.
Foreign investors also took flight after the authorities hanged nine activists, including author Ken Saro Wiwa in 1995.
American pharmaceutical firm Pfizer was the latest to disinvest after successful management buy-out by its Nigerian officials who changed its name to Neimeth International Pharmaceuticals Plc.
Other firms already doing business in the country scaled down on expansion plans with heavy consequences for jobs, according economic analysts.

There was widespread disappointment when in January the government failed to announce the commencement of a much-awaited privatisation which the World Bank as well as local and foreign investors believe will bring back foreign investment.
